b: Hermione Lee’s Anita Brookner: Life and Art, James Gleick’s The Telephone, and Gerald Martin’s Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life all feature among the best reviewed nonfiction titles of the month.
Brought to you by Book Marks, Lit Hub’s home for book reviews.

1. Anita Brookner: Art and Life by Hermione Lee
(Knopf)

12 Rave • 4 Positive
Read an excerpt from Anita Brookner: Art and Life here

“Offers a passionate case for studying this complex, compelling, now obscure figure … For readers who’ve ever felt similarly dismissed, the biography may spark a new passion for this connoisseur of women’s interior lives, a writer who could see what many did not.”

2. The Intangibles: Friendship, Fatherhood, and the Love of the Game by Nick Paumgarten
(Penguin)
“Inventive … Vivid … Hockey fans will adore this, and more casual readers will be charmed by Paumgarten’s thoughtful examinations of manhood. It’s a winner.”

3. The Telephone: A New History by James Gleick
(Farrar, Straus and Giroux)

5 Rave • 4 Positive
Read an excerpt from The Telephone here

“James Gleick’s latest book, The Telephone, restores the old instrument to its rightful place in history. And, furthermore, it burnishes a once mundane tool with dignity and mystique … Gleick is a respected science writer who likes to get out of the lab onto those streets and beyond, with a touch of Doc and his DeLorean from Back to the Future … This elegant survey should be required reading for digital natives.”

4. Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life by Gerald Martin
(Bloomsbury)

“Remarkable … Martin’s assessments of Vargas Llosa’s books vary widely, but his praise of the ‘truly great’ writer is consistent. He is loyal to the man too, but that loyalty is more critical, and it is hard sometimes to see that the life and the books have much in common. Perhaps they don’t. And perhaps this biography is all the better for that reason … Martin understands perfectly that to explain is often to explain away.”
–Michael Wood (The New York Times Book Review)

5. The King Under the Mountain: In Search of J. R. R. Tolkien by D. J. Taylor
(Pegasus)

5 Rave • 1 Positive • 3 Mixed
Read an excerpt from The King Under the Mountain here

“Freed from the obligations of biography, Taylor offers instead a wittier, shorter and more irreverent book that traces Tolkien’s life, while grappling with the mysteries and contradictions of his personality and his achievements … Thorough, insightful and deeply researched, The King Under The Mountain manages to smile at Tolkien’s quirks and absurdities while paying tribute to his mysterious and undoubted gift.”
